title: The tilma of Guadalupe
hookLine: the image shows a pregnant Indigenous woman standing before the sun

cards: Her hands are pressed together. Her head tilts down and a little to one side, eyes lowered, as if she's listening to someone shorter than she is. Rays of light pour out all around her.
Under her feet is a dark crescent moon, held up by a small angel. Her mantle is blue-green and scattered with stars.
This is the image on the tilma, the rough cloak of a man named Juan Diego, kept today in the basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City. You heard the story of the roses he carried in it back in year one.
Today, just the picture, looked at slowly.

teach.b: First, the light and the moon. Catholic readers hear in this image a vision from the last book of the Bible. In the Douay-Rheims, John sees "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet."
The tilma looks like that line, painted. Second, her face. Her skin is dark, and her features are those of a native woman of that land, like Juan Diego himself, an Indigenous man.
She doesn't look like a visitor from far away; she looks like the people who first gathered to see her.

teach.h: A BAND AT HER WAIST: SHE IS WITH CHILD.
teach.b: Third, the dark band tied above her belly. Some readers see in it the sign of a woman expecting a child.

If they're right, the one the picture is really about is hidden: not on her arm, as in the icon from Poland, but within her. Elizabeth's greeting in Luke's Gospel says it: "blessed is the fruit of thy womb."

teach.h: SHE STANDS BEFORE THE SUN, AND PRAYS.
teach.b: She stands in front of the sun, and she prays.

teach.h: BLESSED IS THE FRUIT OF THY WOMB.
teach.b: Some readers say the picture spoke clearly to people who had honored the sun: here is a woman greater than the sun, and she bows her head to someone greater still.
And yesterday's rule holds: no Catholic is required to believe the cloak is miraculous. Pilgrims come anyway, to look.

how: Catholics venerate the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe on Juan Diego's tilma, which hangs in the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City; pilgrims come to look at it and pray, and copies of the image hang in churches and homes across the Americas.

games.q: what does “the tilma of guadalupe” mean?
o: a Mexican shawl worn by pilgrims to the basilica
the starry blue-green mantle on a Mary statue
Juan Diego's cloak bearing the image of Mary

games.q: the tilma of Guadalupe — tap the pairs.
p: a crescent moon and an angel
the dark band at her waist
read as a sign she is with child

s: on the tilma, Mary holds the child on her arm
no child is shown. some readers see the band at her waist as the sign she is carrying him within her.
the image echoes the woman clothed with the sun
Apocalypse 12:1: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet."
Catholics are required to believe the tilma is miraculous
like every private revelation, it may be honored but is never required belief.

games.q: you're making an image of Mary for people who have only just heard of her son. how do you show her?
o: as a foreign queen on a high throne.
as a woman who looks like them, praying, with a child on the way.
as a figure greater than everyone, with no one above her.
games.why: the tilma shows a native woman of that land, head bowed in prayer, standing before the sun, and, some readers say, carrying her child: she points past herself.

practice: If you can, find a picture of the tilma; if not, let today's description stand in.
Go slowly from the bottom up, one breath for each: the angel, the moon, the hem of her dress, her hands, her lowered eyes, then come back down to the band at her waist and stay there.
If you pray, say the Hail Mary slowly and stop at the fruit of thy womb; if not, simply keep looking.

wordCard.voice: The tilma of Guadalupe. Juan Diego's cloak, with its image of Mary as a native woman standing before the sun, praying, and, some readers say, carrying her child. Today's word, and the end of this week.

orig.note: Latin, from Luke 1:42 and the Hail Mary: the fruit of thy womb.

carryVoice: Your line: she carries him. The one the picture is about is hidden inside it. One thousand three hundred forty-four days now.
